talks.title: Galactic Hacker Party To WHY2025: The History, Future & Importance Of NL Hacker Camps
talks.teaser: Traces the Dutch hacker camp scene from its earliest days to today, and why these volunteer-run events matter.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a volunteer in the Dutch hacker camp scene, walks through the history of these events, starting with an early Dutch hacker magazine from the mid-1980s. He describes how the first gathering, the Galactic Hacker Party, was promoted with viral-style flyers and aimed at technically curious people. Later camps added their own experiments, such as a network built inside an outdoor toilet, while police and municipalities sometimes warned organisers and sometimes let events go ahead.

Across the following decades the camps grew, with talks from one early edition still available online and a cable-cutting warning recalled from an early event. The speaker links the camp scene to the rise of hacker spaces in the Netherlands, which followed a 2009 camp, and to projects that came out of the events, including a basic-security check of municipalities and a Corona notification app effort during the pandemic.

He closes with the upcoming anniversary edition, planned for August near Geest Ambacht with around 300 visitors, and asks for volunteers and talk proposals across its areas and teams. The takeaway is that these volunteer-run gatherings build community, trust and practical initiatives, and that newcomers can join through the mailing list or the socials.

talks.title: Inside Job: Tackling Insider Risk From All Angles
talks.teaser: Maps how intentional insiders are pushed toward harm and why layered controls, monitoring and culture all matter.
talks.summary:
Insider risk is defined as the threat from current or former employees, contractors or anyone with access to critical networks, systems, data or people, and it affects every industry. The speakers note that organizations often feel secure while underestimating the cost, which reaches legal fees, regulatory penalties, higher insurance and lost customers. Roughly half of incidents are unintentional, such as falling for a phishing link, while about a quarter are intentional and usually do the most damage.

The session centres on intentional insiders, tracing a research-based pathway from personal traits and personal or work stressors to concerning behaviour, then the organization's response, and finally the malicious act. Motives include money, disgruntlement, professional gain and ideology. One case involved an engineer who was paid to hand over a full software source code; warning signs were ignored, and the company lost its main customer and much of its market value. The speakers then review common controls such as access management, monitoring, pre-employment screening, NDAs and awareness training, highlighting pitfalls like access kept after people leave, alert overload and training that only ticks compliance boxes.

They close with a holistic approach: leadership-backed governance, starting with critical assets and people, a narrative framed as trust but verify, behaviour-focused training, a mix of tools and trained staff, and a culture that supports employees in trouble. Their message is that the question is not whether an insider incident happens but how often.

talks.title: When Artificial Becomes Authentic, How Do I Prove I Am Me?
talks.teaser: Explains how voice clones and deepfakes make impersonation harder to disprove, and why verifying identity needs new habits.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with the speaker's early research on digital identity theft and a 2008 case in the Netherlands, where a man whose personal information had been misused struggled to be believed. It highlights a recurring problem for victims of impersonation: they are often expected to prove they did not do something, while records in databases are assumed to be correct.

Drawing on later work assessing cybercrime threats for a European law enforcement agency, the speaker argues that criminals mostly adapt familiar tactics, and that generative AI mainly makes social engineering faster and more convincing. Examples include an employee at a company who was tricked by a deepfake video call into a large money transfer, a late-night call using a cloned mother's voice to demand money, and fake North Korean IT workers who used existing American identities to get hired at more than 300 companies. A school principal's cloned voice was also used to make racist remarks that he said he never made.

The speaker is skeptical that technology alone, criminalising the tools, or public awareness that teaches people to spot fakes will solve the problem, since detection keeps lagging and people cannot reliably recognise clones. She argues for a zero-trust mindset in which identity is treated as possibly inauthentic until verified, using other channels such as asking questions or agreeing on a family password shared in person. She closes by asking how people will prove who they are in the future.

talks.title: Build Your Own Role-playing Game: The Business Continuity Drill
talks.teaser: Walks through a ten-step method for designing and running a tabletop business continuity drill as a role-playing game.
talks.summary:
The talk explains what a business continuity plan contains, including its purpose, activation criteria, roles, processes and contact details, and why a tabletop drill is a safer way to test it than simulating an outage on production systems. The speaker presents a ten-step method for building a drill that runs like a role-playing game, with a game master, players, actors and observers.

The steps cover defining what the drill should test, such as whether people follow their role descriptions, recognise when the activation criteria are met, or hold the plan in memory. Organisers then choose a scenario, often made bigger for learning, and an environment. The first drill ran in a meeting room, which felt artificial, so the second used a dedicated workspace that mirrored the company's own, with participants joining at different times. Scripts include participant briefings, timelines with milestones, and prompts to unblock players, such as sending the plan by email when a simulated Google Drive outage hid it, or posting staged angry customer messages. A test run with engineers, a recording and a scoring form help organisers.

The closing advice is to keep the drill focused on process, collaboration and the plan rather than deep technical knowledge, and to keep it engaging so people want to return. Debriefs should feed follow-up actions into backlogs and plan updates. The speaker argues that a manual drill can still be meaningful and can help win support for reliability and security work.

talks.title: Hacking The Vote: Why The Paper Trail Matters In Elections
talks.teaser: Explains why the Netherlands dropped voting machines and why a verifiable paper trail matters for trustworthy elections.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why the Netherlands stopped using electronic voting machines and how its election process is meant to stay trustworthy. Fleur Van Leusden, who works for the Dutch electoral council, a government advisory body and election authority, starts with the principles the country follows: voting secrecy, accessibility, integrity, one vote per person, transparency and verifiability, and independence from government. She describes how the machines worked, with candidate buttons and a red confirm button, and how these principles came out of research by government commissions.

The main case is the downfall of the machines. A group of hackers examined the device and showed that swapping a chip could make it change results. They bought the locks that protected the machines online for about a euro each, handed the keys to journalists at a press conference, and showed the machines could be opened. Other problems were weak storage security, certification that covered the machine but not the equipment around it, a reprint that was not a true recount, and closed-source software that no one could inspect. Tempest radiation could also reveal how someone voted, which led to a change in the law. Lawsuits followed, and the machines were taken out of use. The speaker then compares barcode and QR ballots and scanners, which bring similar transparency problems, and notes that paper has its own weaknesses, such as ballot stuffing and proxy voting.

The talk closes with the view that paper is not perfect but is easier to check, and that voting machines are costly to replace every few years. In questions, the speaker discussed US voting systems, disinformation, and the council's practice of publishing penetration test reports before each election. The takeaway is that a visible paper trail and public verification are what keep elections trustworthy.

talks.title: Turning Neurodiversity Into A Strength
talks.teaser: Shows how neurodiverse people's strengths fit security work, and how employers can open paths for them beyond diplomas.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why neurodiverse people, including those with autism or ADHD, are often passed over for cyber security roles despite strengths such as attention to detail, pattern recognition and persistence. The speaker, who learned she is autistic at 35, shares her own path: leaving school early, working in hospitality, writing letters for years to win a job at one company, and moving from help desk to Windows system administration and application management before burnout led to a diagnosis.

After that she describes applying for security jobs for about three years and being turned down because she lacked a high school diploma, even when she offered to prove her skills another way. She argues that employers should judge skills over diplomas, offer trial periods, and set clear career pathways with certificates and learning goals. She also covers workplace needs such as clear communication, quiet workspaces, routine and structure, and teams that understand each other's working styles, and she warns that masking, the effort of hiding who you are, can lead to burnout.

In the question round she encourages neurodiverse people to disclose their needs so HR can act on them, and suggests that managers look first at existing staff in help desk and administration roles who may be ready to grow. She closes by asking listeners to question why their own organisations do not hire neurodiverse people.

talks.title: Keynote: Spooky Action
talks.teaser: Explains how quantum computers threaten current encryption and how organisations can start preparing now.
talks.summary:
This keynote by Jaya Baloo starts with the idea that foundational, connecting science often matters more than any single part, then turns to quantum computing and why it matters for security. The talk covers why Moore's law is tapering off, how qubits and entanglement grow computing power, and why the public-key schemes built on integer factorization and discrete logarithms would fall to Shor's and Grover's algorithms once large enough quantum machines exist. It also describes the harvest-now, decrypt-later problem, where encrypted traffic is collected today and stored until it can be broken.

The speaker argues that organisations are poor at changing cryptography and that few know which algorithms they run. Quantum key distribution is presented as useful only at specific points in a network, because it depends on dedicated links, and a 2016 Chinese satellite experiment is cited as an example of what has been achieved. A caution follows about a post-quantum candidate that was broken on an old classical computer, which fuelled fear and doubt, and against rolling your own cryptography.

The practical advice is to treat cryptography as an asset, inventory it, raise key lengths on current algorithms, and pilot post-quantum options with vendors while asking suppliers for their roadmaps through third-party risk processes. Basics such as knowing your network, managing vulnerabilities and threat modelling should come first. The talk closes by urging a sense of urgency that stays grounded in real threat evaluation rather than panic.

talks.title: Tools Vs Rules: Why Technical Based Measures Work Better Than Behavior Based
talks.teaser: Explains why technical measures usually beat policy-only rules for managing risk, with workplace examples and CISO advice.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common reflex in security: treating a risk as handled once a rule forbids something. The speaker, a CISO who previously worked as a software test engineer, recalls risk workshops where colleagues answered a torrent-download concern with "just make a rule." She also cites a case where two former Tesla employees shared internal information with a media outlet despite policy. Tesla only learned of it when journalists got in touch, because it had no technical means to detect or block the leak.

She argues that rules are cheap and easy to write, but people still break them for many reasons, from not knowing the rule to missing a deadline. Using balcony railings as an analogy, she says controls reduce the chance and impact of mistakes even if they cannot remove them entirely. Her preferred model combines both: a policy explains why something is blocked, and a technical measure enforces it, which also shifts responsibility to anyone who circumvents it. Awareness work helps most when it explains reasons and offers approved alternatives to reduce shadow IT.

In the Q&A she covers residual risk, malicious compliance and culture change, which she says must start at the top. She keeps a one-page security vision that prefers technical measures, which can help when budget is tight. She concludes that rules aimed at executives are harder to enforce technically, so agreements should be written down.

talks.title: Anti Surveillance Knitting
talks.teaser: A knitted jumper floods older face detection methods with false positives, but does not make its wearer invisible.
talks.summary: The speaker explains how facial detection algorithms identify faces, then describes designing and knitting a patterned jumper to trigger false detections. Testing with OpenCV and VF Frame produced false positives, though the approach targets older detection methods and does not prevent surveillance or hide the wearer’s face.
